title: US Energy Agency Announces Wave Energy Prize Competition
main_content:
Sun and wind are seen as the most abundant sources of clean, renewable energy, but as many ‘ocean-hugging’ countries know, the energy of ocean waves is also both powerful and endless. Looking for the most efficient ways to capture that energy, the U.S. Department of Energy has announced a $1.5 million-prize competition for new ideas.

The department estimates that waves and tides along the U.S. coasts generate 1,420 terawatt-hours of energy annually. That is equal to the output of more than 330 nuclear power plants.

Unfortunately, the efficiency of today’s technologies for capturing that energy is only about 20 percent, too low for the investment to be economical, says Jose Zayas, director of the Wind and Water Power Technologies Office at the Department of Energy.

Competition organizers expect that most of the new ideas will be coming from existing energy companies, but also from the academic sector and research institutions.

Zayas says the ultimate goal of the Wave Energy Prize is to inspire a new set of power-generating technologies for the 21st century. Developers of the three best performing devices will be awarded prizes ranging from $250,000 to $1.5 million.

questions.question: What is the competition about?
options: Developing new solar panel designs for better energy capture
Creating innovative methods to harness wave energy more efficiently
Increasing the output of nuclear power plants along the coast
Formulating strategies to decrease the cost of fossil fuel energy
questions.answer: Creating innovative methods to harness wave energy more efficiently

questions.question: How powerful are the waves and tides along the US coasts?
options: They generate energy equivalent to 100 nuclear power plants annually.
They produce about 500 terawatt-hours of energy each year.
They generate approximately 1,420 terawatt-hours of energy annually.
They are not capable of generating significant amounts of energy.
questions.answer: They generate approximately 1,420 terawatt-hours of energy annually.

questions.question: How efficient are today’s technologies in capturing the ocean’s energy?
options: They are about 50 percent efficient, making them quite effective.
They achieve an efficiency of approximately 20 percent.
They have reached an efficiency level of 40 percent in recent developments.
They are nearly 100 percent efficient, capturing most of the energy available.
questions.answer: They achieve an efficiency of approximately 20 percent.
